frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and export infrastructure, but European buyers seek diversification and greater pricing leverage. Pipeline and LNG ties with Italy and Spain remain strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases pressure on Algeria's borders and complicates regional diplomacy. External military and commercial competition in the Sahel challenges Algiers' preference for non-intervention.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic finance
frictionVectors.details: Angola is reducing dependence on Chinese financing while remaining exposed to oil-backed debt, international lenders, and foreign operators. This limits policy autonomy despite efforts to strengthen domestic participation.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: US, European, and Chinese interests are converging around the Lobito rail corridor and access to critical minerals from the wider Copperbelt. Infrastructure investment offers diversification but risks converting Angola into a transit platform for external supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port and logistics economy remains highly tied to Nigerian commerce and regional transit rules. Infrastructure expansion involving foreign contractors and financiers could deepen dependence if domestic value capture remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel insurgency frontier
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity along the northern borders threatens transport corridors, protected areas, and agricultural production. Security cooperation with external partners is increasing, but it also exposes Benin to competing regional and international agendas.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater domestic value addition and a larger share of diamond revenues in its relationship with De Beers. The central risk is that prolonged commercial tension could weaken market access or investment.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals is growing as investors seek alternatives to concentrated supply chains. Gaborone retains strong regulatory capacity but must balance investment attraction with sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking tighter control over gold production, licensing, and refining while reducing the role of Western firms. Greater state capture may increase fiscal control, but weak oversight and insecurity could encourage illicit extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's reliance on Russian-linked security support has displaced several Western partnerships without resolving the insurgency. This creates new dependencies around security access, mining concessions, and political influence.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, gold, and rare-metal projects, but weak institutions and limited financing leave it dependent on foreign operators and opaque contract renegotiations.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern DRC constrain trade and infrastructure links while increasing reliance on external diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, airports, and maritime services is strategically valuable but creates exposure to competing European, Chinese, and transatlantic interests.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde retains strong institutional control, yet its vast maritime zone and Atlantic location require continued external support for surveillance, anti-trafficking, and undersea infrastructure protection.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain central to roads, power, and port development, increasing external leverage over strategic infrastructure and repayment priorities.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND BORDER INSTABILITY
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict and insecurity near Nigeria and the Central African Republic disrupt transport corridors, weaken local resource governance, and raise operating costs for extractive projects.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-MINING LINKAGE
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel remain closely associated with regime protection and access to gold and diamond concessions, limiting transparency and bargaining space for the state.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND BORDER VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecure borders with Sudan, Chad, and the DRC make mineral exports dependent on foreign-controlled or politically exposed transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE AND OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chad relies heavily on oil revenue and the Cameroon export corridor, leaving national fiscal sovereignty vulnerable to foreign operators, price shocks, and transit disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY REALIGNMENT
frictionVectors.details: The transition away from traditional French security reliance occurs amid Sudan-war spillover and expanding Gulf and Russian diplomatic interest, complicating control over borders and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Maritime Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte remains the country’s central sovereignty grievance and complicates migration, maritime jurisdiction, and bilateral cooperation with France.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Dependence on Ports and Energy
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal capacity leaves transport, electricity, and port modernization dependent on external donors and Gulf, French, or multilateral financing.

frictionVectors.title: M23–Rwanda Security Crisis
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa’s territorial authority and expose mineral corridors to regional and transnational influence.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Bargaining Pressure
frictionVectors.details: China, Western governments, and international mining firms compete for access to strategic minerals, while the state seeks stronger local processing, revenue capture, and contract leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on offshore oil leaves fiscal sovereignty exposed to price cycles and foreign operators, with limited diversification into higher-value domestic industries.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing remain important to transport and urban development, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Processing and External Buyers
frictionVectors.details: The government is expanding domestic processing and producer oversight, but global traders and price volatility still constrain national control over cocoa revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Northern border areas face risks from militant infiltration and instability in Burkina Faso and Mali, increasing security costs and dependence on external intelligence and defense partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Basing
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provides revenue and deterrence but limits Djibouti’s strategic autonomy and makes it a target in wider rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port infrastructure and competition with alternative Red Sea and Horn logistics hubs create debt, commercial, and bargaining pressures around national infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Asset Exposure
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf investment provide financial relief but increase external influence over ports, land, and state-linked enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt dependent on diplomacy and regional partnerships to protect downstream water security.

highlights: Oil rents remain the regime's fiscal anchor

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields reduce state revenue and increase pressure to attract foreign technical and financial partners.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Limited transparency around hydrocarbons and infrastructure contracts weakens public oversight and leaves the economy exposed to external operators.

highlights: State control over strategic assets remains tight

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide foreign exchange but give a small number of external partners disproportionate influence over export earnings and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline remains strategically valuable as regional powers compete for access, while sanctions history and diplomatic isolation constrain investment choices.

highlights: South African dependence shapes economic sovereignty
Sugar and textile exports retain limited leverage

frictionVectors.title: Regional Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Energy, transport, finance, and consumer supply chains remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Mbabane's room for autonomous economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Export Preference Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and apparel sectors depend heavily on external market access and trade preferences, making employment and fiscal stability sensitive to policy changes abroad.

highlights: Debt and conflict constrain sovereign consolidation

frictionVectors.title: Nile Dam Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The GERD gives Ethiopia greater control over electricity generation and regional diplomacy, but unresolved operating rules continue to provoke Egyptian and Sudanese opposition.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Strategic Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for port and trade access create leverage for Gulf, Chinese, Western, and neighboring-state actors over infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: French influence recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking more diversified partnerships while reducing dependence on traditional French security and commercial networks. The transition government’s nationalist posture could complicate established contracts and political ties.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain central to manganese extraction, rail logistics, and port operations. Gabon is attempting to capture more processing value, but infrastructure and financing limits constrain leverage.

highlights: Fisheries and port access under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport connectivity, trade routes, and regional security. This provides stability but limits Banjul’s room for independent infrastructure and customs policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign-linked fishing activity continues to challenge enforcement of Gambian waters and local food security. Weak monitoring capacity leaves licensing revenue and marine resources vulnerable to external exploitation.

highlights: Galamsey threatens water and mining governance

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold-mining networks
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining, including activity linked to foreign operators, is degrading water systems and weakening state control over gold production. Enforcement faces resistance from local political and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and extractive-sector leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed fiscal reforms and debt restructuring restrict Accra’s policy flexibility in oil, gold, and emerging lithium projects. The government is seeking greater domestic value capture while remaining dependent on foreign capital and commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and multinational investment into rail, port, and mine infrastructure. Guinea may gain export revenue, but foreign-controlled logistics could limit sovereign control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite enclave economics
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate much of Guinea’s bauxite production and transport, while environmental costs and limited local processing remain contentious. The junta’s contract reviews and local-content demands risk clashes with investors.

highlights: Cashew and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-market dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on cashew exports, with foreign traders and processors capturing substantial value. Limited domestic processing leaves the sector vulnerable to price shocks and external commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries access and maritime enforcement
frictionVectors.details: European and Asian fishing interests compete for access to Guinea-Bissau’s productive waters. Weak maritime surveillance and governance capacity reduce the state’s ability to secure sustainable catches and transparent licensing revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Kenya remains dependent on IMF support, concessional lenders, and commercial refinancing, limiting policy autonomy. Public resistance to tax increases reflects concern that debt servicing is displacing domestic development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains strategically important to regional trade, while Gulf, Chinese, and Western actors compete for influence over ports, logistics, and infrastructure. Kenya is balancing diversification against the risk of long-term strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria and expose Lesotho to delays, cost overruns, and unequal bargaining power. Hydropower and compensation disputes remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Political Instability and External Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Coalition politics and weak institutions constrain Lesotho's ability to negotiate consistently with South Africa, donors, and private investors. Economic dependence leaves the kingdom vulnerable to external pressure over security, migration, and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations are central to export earnings but concentrate infrastructure, employment, and fiscal benefits in foreign-controlled concession structures. The government faces pressure to improve local content, taxation, and community compensation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders retain significant influence over port facilities, mining railways, and export corridors. Liberia is seeking investment while attempting to prevent strategic infrastructure from becoming detached from national development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest access to state institutions, petroleum revenues, and production infrastructure. Foreign energy interests benefit from continued exports but also reinforce fragmented bargaining among domestic factions.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Mercenary Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors retain overlapping security and political interests in Libya. Their involvement constrains unified national decision-making and keeps strategic infrastructure exposed to coercion.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects attract major foreign capital but provide Madagascar with limited leverage over processing, pricing, and downstream value. Fiscal and environmental disputes remain acute around large concession areas.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Port Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and constrained transport networks increase dependence on foreign operators, donors, and project-finance institutions. Mining corridors and port upgrades risk serving export enclaves unless connected to broader domestic industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: IMF AUSTERITY AND IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit fiscal room while Malawi remains dependent on external financing, fuel, fertilizer, and food imports.

frictionVectors.title: MINING INVESTMENT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects attract foreign capital, but weak regulatory capacity creates risks of limited domestic value capture and environmental stress.

highlights: Junta deepens strategic rupture with the West

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Bamako relies increasingly on Russian-linked security support after breaking with France and regional institutions, trading strategic access and political alignment for military assistance.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND TERRITORIAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the country’s principal hard-currency asset, but insecurity, informal mining, and disputes over mining terms limit transparent sovereign control and public revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: GTA GAS PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The offshore Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal strengthens Mauritania’s revenue outlook but leaves early gas-sector development dependent on foreign operators, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND CORRIDOR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in iron ore, green hydrogen, ports, and rail can diversify the economy, but external lenders and operators retain substantial influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND BASE POLITICS
frictionVectors.details: The future of the Chagos Archipelago and the Diego Garcia military facility remains a sensitive sovereignty issue involving the United Kingdom, the United States, and Mauritius.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners compete for influence through ports, finance, fisheries, and maritime-security cooperation, testing Mauritius’s balancing strategy.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty contest

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, renewable energy, and transport projects in Western Sahara remain tied to Morocco’s sovereignty claims and face diplomatic and legal challenges.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INDUSTRIAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, Gulf, and North American capital supports automotive, energy, logistics, and infrastructure expansion, but also creates exposure to external market and technology leverage.

highlights: LNG restart remains central to national recovery
Cabo Delgado security still limits sovereign control

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and external security support remain essential to protecting Cabo Delgado gas projects. This limits Maputo's operational autonomy and exposes revenues to delays and renegotiation.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and Development Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity continues to threaten transport corridors, local legitimacy, and resource infrastructure. Northern communities remain skeptical that offshore gas wealth will produce broad-based benefits.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries are attracting major foreign operators while Windhoek seeks stronger state participation, taxation, and local procurement. Contract design will determine whether the sector builds domestic capability or reproduces enclave extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on foreign capital, export infrastructure, and access to land and water. Negotiations over community benefits and public guarantees could become a major sovereignty issue.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil policy

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Concession Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Niamey's confrontation with foreign uranium interests reflects a push for greater national control over strategic minerals. The dispute risks production losses, litigation, and reduced technical access.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Resource Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Growing reliance on Russian security cooperation may reduce Western leverage but creates new dependence on an external patron. Limited financing and technical capacity could constrain Niger's ability to convert political control into reliable resource revenues.

highlights: Oil theft still erodes national capture

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Infrastructure Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and community grievances continue to reduce state receipts and deter investment. Foreign operators are divesting some mature assets, leaving the government with difficult remediation and security burdens.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Fuel-Market Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery improves Nigeria's potential control over fuel supply, but disputes involving regulators, importers, and national oil institutions remain politically sensitive. Pricing and crude-access rules will determine whether refining capacity translates into durable sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces persistent international accusations that cross-border networks linked to the M23 conflict facilitate mineral flows from eastern DRC. Diplomatic pressure and possible sanctions could affect Rwanda's mineral exports and external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong domestic state capacity coexists with reliance on foreign aid, concessional finance, and external security relationships. Shifts in donor policy could narrow Kigali's room to maneuver on regional security and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Offshore oil hopes remain commercially unproven
Maritime security is a strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe relies on foreign capital and technical expertise for exploration in its offshore blocks, limiting near-term bargaining power. Uncertain discoveries have constrained government revenues and leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime crime threaten control over the country's extensive maritime zone. The government remains dependent on regional and external naval cooperation for surveillance and enforcement.

highlights: New hydrocarbons strengthen state bargaining power
Resource nationalism is testing investor confidence

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater transparency, domestic participation, and fiscal returns from offshore oil and gas projects involving international operators. Renegotiation pressure could improve sovereign control but create friction with investors.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dakar and competing logistics corridors is drawing financing and strategic interest from Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish actors. Senegal must balance infrastructure access with concerns over long-term concessions and debt exposure.

highlights: Foreign fishing pressure challenges maritime control

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has comparatively strong marine governance but limited capacity to monitor its vast exclusive economic zone. Foreign fishing access and illegal, unreported, and unregulated activity continue to test enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE AND CLIMATE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on international finance, tourism, and climate-related support for resilient infrastructure. This creates leverage for external lenders and donors even as Seychelles maintains substantial policy autonomy.

highlights: Mining growth is outpacing domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and other minerals attract foreign operators whose capital and logistics dominate production. Weak downstream processing and revenue-management capacity leave Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and unequal value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL FINANCING
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked ports, roads, and rail corridors are increasingly shaped by external investors and lenders. These projects can improve export capacity while locking strategic infrastructure into concession structures that limit policy flexibility.

highlights: Maritime assets are becoming central to sovereignty
Security dependence limits control over resources

frictionVectors.title: PORT ACCESS AND EXTERNAL SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners retain major influence through port, training, and security arrangements. These relationships strengthen state capacity but can fragment national control over strategic maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCES AND FEDERAL DISPUTES
frictionVectors.details: Potential offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries remain constrained by insecurity, weak licensing capacity, and disputes between the federal government and member states. External operators face elevated political and security risk, limiting Somalia's immediate bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and weak freight infrastructure constrain domestic control over mineral value chains. Foreign capital remains important for extraction, logistics, and energy transition projects.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals alignment
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is balancing Western investment, BRICS partnerships, and demands for local beneficiation without fully committing to either bloc.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving oil revenues hostage to external transit risks and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector capture
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation, armed insecurity, and opaque contracting limit sovereign control over production and public revenue. Foreign operators remain central to technical capacity and market access.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic assets
Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance competing armed networks while foreign intermediaries and regional patrons capture significant value outside formal state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea competition
frictionVectors.details: Port access and military-logistics ties draw competing external interest, reducing Khartoum's ability to manage infrastructure and maritime resources on sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: The government is demanding greater local participation, fiscal returns, and processing from foreign mining firms, creating periodic disputes over licensing and project terms.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and LNG dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major rail, port, and prospective gas investments bring financing and connectivity but could deepen reliance on foreign operators and lenders if domestic value capture remains limited.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's strategic port and logistics networks depend heavily on foreign capital, operators, and regional trade flows, exposing sovereignty to commercial and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate production provides strategic revenue but limited downstream transformation, leaving the country vulnerable to commodity-price swings and external market control.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance remains strong against perceived externalization of European border controls.

frictionVectors.title: Stalled Resource Reform
frictionVectors.details: Weak investment and fiscal pressure limit Tunisia's ability to modernize phosphate production and reduce energy-import dependence. Delayed external financing further narrows policy autonomy.

highlights: China and Gulf capital expand footprint

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed, TotalEnergies-linked oil pipeline is central to Uganda's export strategy but faces environmental, financing, and human-rights opposition. Reliance on external capital and infrastructure partners limits Kampala's control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign lenders and contractors remain important across transport, energy, and digital infrastructure. Debt-servicing needs increase exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and Western bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Value-Chain Contest
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater local processing and stronger fiscal returns from copper while competing investors pursue long-term control of mines and logistics. Power shortages and rail constraints still weaken Lusaka's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Conditions
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms have stabilized access to finance but constrain spending and industrial-policy flexibility. Western creditors, Chinese lenders, and mining investors retain substantial influence over economic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on raw lithium exports to capture more domestic value, but Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in mining and processing. Limited capital, technology, and infrastructure keep the country dependent on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Investment Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and governance disputes restrict financing options, while Harare increasingly relies on non-Western investors and mineral-backed deals. This narrows economic choice and increases exposure to opaque extraction arrangements.
